analysis.one_liner: Requires colleges to publish real graduation, debt, and earnings outcomes for every program.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan transparency bill from Sens. Wyden, Rubio, and Warner was referred to the Senate education committee the day it was introduced in March 2019 and never received a hearing, vote, or any further action before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would build a new federal higher education data system that tracks, for every college and every program of study, how many students graduate, how much federal loan debt they carry, and what they earn 2, 6, and 15 years after leaving. Those numbers would be published on the Department of Education's website and broken out by Pell Grant status, race, gender, age, first-generation status, veteran status, and enrollment pattern. Colleges would have to link to the data from their own cost and financial aid pages, so students could see the actual payoff of a program before enrolling or borrowing. The bill specifies privacy-protecting technology so no individual student's records could be identified by the government or anyone else.
analysis.who_benefits: Students and families deciding where to enroll and how much to borrow, including Pell Grant recipients, part-time and adult students, and veterans using education benefits, who today often cannot find program-level graduation, debt, and earnings numbers before committing. Taxpayers also gain a way to see which programs deliver on the federal aid dollars flowing to them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Students choosing colleges and taking on debt

how_it_helps.text: The bill requires outcome metrics — completion rates, mean and median federal loan debt including accrued interest, loan repayment rates, dropout rates, and earnings and debt-to-earnings ratios at 2, 6, and 15 years after exit — calculated for each participating institution and, where feasible, each program of study, not just each campus [S3].

The metrics must be disaggregated by categories including Pell Grant receipt, loan status, veteran and servicemember status, race or ethnicity, age, gender, first-generation status, and enrollment status, so the outcomes for the exact kind of student considering a program are visible rather than hidden in averages [S3].

The Department must publish the metrics on its website in a user-friendly, machine-readable format, and within five years every participating college must display a clear link to that data on any webpage with cost, financial aid, or admissions information [S3].

The system must use privacy-protecting technology so that raw student-level data, including personally identifiable information, is not accessible to the Department or any other party, no individual can be identified, and the Department is barred from selling any of the collected data [S3].

Earnings data would come directly from the Social Security Administration and the Treasury for workers, the self-employed, independent contractors, and military members, replacing the reliance on narrow, incomplete graduate surveys [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and programs with weak graduation, debt, and earnings outcomes — including for-profit and low-completion programs — would face public exposure of numbers they do not currently have to show. Taxpayers would fund building and running the system through fiscal year 2028.
analysis.who_pays_short: Colleges with poor graduation and earnings outcomes

drawbacks.text: The system links student enrollment records to Social Security and Treasury earnings data for every federal aid recipient, a national student-level tracking mechanism; the bill responds with secure computation technology and access limits, but it still centralizes sensitive earnings and education data at the federal level [S3].

Earnings measured only two years after program completion can mislead: students who continue on to further degrees, or who enter lower-paying fields such as teaching or public service, would initially show low earnings even if their later outcomes are strong — the bill mitigates this by also requiring 6- and 15-year figures [S3].

The bill authorizes open-ended appropriations ('such sums as may be necessary') for fiscal years 2020 through 2028 with no cost estimate, and the transition from the existing IPEDS reporting system would take years to complete [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — letting students see, before borrowing, what a specific program actually delivers for people like them — directly targets the situation of the roughly 43 million Americans carrying federal student loan debt, and the privacy design in the bill is more protective than most federal data programs. The main costs are real but bounded: a one-time federal data infrastructure build, and public embarrassment for weak programs, which is the point. The earnings-at-two-years measurement could unfairly brand some worthwhile programs, though the 15-year figures temper that. On balance a well-designed transparency measure whose main cost falls on institutions that benefit from students not knowing the numbers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate education committee the same day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: S. 681 was introduced on March 6, 2019 by Sen. Ron Wyden with Sens. Marco Rubio and Mark Warner, giving it one Republican and one Democratic cosponsor [S3][S4].

It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day, and the action history shows no further action of any kind — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The institutions — particularly low-completion and low-earnings programs, including parts of the for-profit college sector — that would have had their program-level debt and earnings outcomes published, and that now continue to enroll and borrow students without that disclosure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Colleges whose weak outcomes would have been published

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken on the bill; its sponsorship was bipartisan (one Democrat and one Republican cosponsor alongside the Democratic sponsor), but the chamber never considered it, so no record shows how the parties would have split.

industries.industry: Colleges with weak outcomes, especially for-profit and low-completion programs
industries.note: The bill would publish program-by-program graduation, debt, and earnings numbers — including transfer and completion rates broken out by whether the destination program is for-profit — that would expose low-value programs to prospective students. These programs profit from federal aid dollars and currently face no requirement to show students the actual payoff before enrollment [S3].

Institutions whose programs genuinely lead to good jobs would get verifiable, government-published evidence of their value, replacing incomplete self-reported graduate surveys, and would also be relieved of duplicative federal reporting once the new system is in place [S3].
